title: India Rejects Patent for Shorter Drug-Resistant TB Treatment BPaL
excerpt: The Patent Office upheld patient-group oppositions against TB Alliance's BPaL application — the six-month, all-oral regimen that replaced 18-24 month courses.
body:
• The Indian Patent Office has rejected TB Alliance's patent application for BPaL, the six-month, all-oral regimen of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
  • The order, dated October 27, followed two pre-grant oppositions filed in 2020 by patient groups, who argued the combination was already known and lacked an inventive step; the office upheld grounds under Sections 3(d), 3(e) and 3(i) of the Patents Act.
  • BPaL replaces older drug-resistant TB courses of 18-24 months that could involve painful injections; the World Health Organization recommends the six-month regimen for eligible patients.
  • For patients: India provides free TB diagnosis and treatment through its national programme — the rejection clears a barrier to generic BPaL supply, but price effects depend on generic makers entering and on procurement.

India's Patent Office has rejected a patent application for the treatment that has changed how drug-resistant tuberculosis is treated. The application, filed by the US-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development (TB Alliance) in April 2018, covered BPaL — a combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, with an option to add pyrazinamide, described as a unitary dosage form. The rejection order is dated October 27, according to The Hindu BusinessLine, and the application was rejected under Section 15 of the Patents Act after TB Alliance did not attend the final hearings. The Hindu's explainer sets out the reasoning in detail.

Why the application failed

The legal question was whether combining three existing medicines into a shorter regimen is an invention. Two pre-grant oppositions, filed in July 2020, said it was not. The first was filed by Eldred Tellis of Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust and Ganesh Acharya, supported by the Lawyers' Collective and the Médecins Sans Frontières Access Campaign. The second came from the Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), supported by the Third World Network. The opponents cited research and clinical trials dating back to 2015 showing the combination and its use were already known, and invoked Section 3(d), which bars patents on new uses of known substances; Section 3(e), on mere admixtures; and Section 3(i), on methods of medical treatment. They also argued the invention was not sufficiently disclosed. The Patent Office upheld the opposition grounds.

"Only those who have been treated for TB know what it feels like to go through more than a year of antibiotics with painful injections."

— Loon Gangte, Delhi Network of Positive People

The burden BPaL is meant to cut

India has the world's largest TB burden: about 2.71 million people developed TB in India in 2024, roughly a quarter of global cases, at an incidence of 187 per 100,000 people. Older treatment for drug-resistant TB ran 18 to 24 months, with multiple medicines and, in some cases, injections. BPaL is six months and all-oral, and the WHO recommends it for eligible patients with certain forms of drug-resistant TB. India's National TB Elimination Programme, introduced in 2020, provides free diagnosis and treatment through public services, and the shorter regimen is already part of programme care in its BPaLM form (with moxifloxacin added).

What the rejection changes — and what it does not

Patient groups welcomed the order as a step that will help facilitate generic competition and improve access to treatment. That mechanism is real but indirect: without a patent on the combination in India, Indian generic manufacturers face one less legal barrier to supplying BPaL, and programme procurement prices can fall if multiple makers compete. The Hindu's explainer cautions that actual savings depend on generic entry, supply and pricing decisions — a patent rejection opens a door; it does not set a price. Civil-society groups also pressed TB Alliance to withdraw or surrender related claims elsewhere and to publish its pretomanid licensing agreements, noting the drug was developed with public and philanthropic support. BPaL-combination patents have been granted in 11 countries, including South Africa, Russia and Indonesia, and run to 2036.

The wider pattern

This is the second major Indian patent decision on a TB medicine in recent years, after the office declined to extend Johnson & Johnson's bedaquiline patent beyond July 2023, opening that drug to generics. Together the decisions define India's position in the global access debate: combinations and new uses of known medicines must clear a high inventive-step bar, especially where the applicant does not contest the opposition. For the 2.71 million people a year who develop TB in India — and for diaspora families funding or supporting treatment back home — the practical test now is procurement: whether programme tenders for BPaL reflect the competition this order makes possible.
